title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest leans into fresh 2026 evidence across your tracked topics — new rapamycin/rapalog dosing trials for anti-aging, a 19-RCT meta-analysis on HIIT for women, a March 2026 pre-surgery pelvic-floor trial, a first-in-class p53 (TP53) reactivator for breast cancer, and the AASM's latest word on treating restless, broken sleep. Sources are linked as chips under each section. Informational only — run anything you'd act on past a clinician first.

sections.topic: Anti-Aging — Rapalogs, Urolithin A & the Dose Question
sections.body:
The 2026 anti-aging story is shifting from *whether* mTOR inhibitors work to *what dose, how often, and in whom* — with an important note that the right dose may differ by sex.

- **Nailing down the dose (RESTOR).** A new NIH/NIA-backed exploratory trial, **RESTOR (NCT06658093)**, began recruiting in **March 2026** to find a safe, intermittent dose of **rapamycin (sirolimus)** and **everolimus** that lowers mTOR activity in older adults toward youthful levels. Notably, the investigators expect the **optimal dose in women to differ from men** — a reminder that longevity dosing shouldn't be one-size-fits-all.
- **A functional-decline RCT.** A separate randomized trial, **NCT05237687**, also started in 2026 to test whether **sirolimus** can move phenotypic and functional biomarkers of aging in older adults.
- **Reality check stands.** A 2026 *Aging (Aging-US)* review reaffirmed there is still **no clear clinical evidence** that low-dose rapamycin extends healthspan or slows aging in healthy adults, despite strong animal data. Rapamycin remains **prescription-only** — it is not a supplement.
- **Cross-over with sleep.** A registered trial, **NCT06990256**, is evaluating the supplements **urolithin A + fisetin** on *both* sleep quality and aging biomarkers — a nice example of the field testing accessible compounds head-to-head with hard endpoints (see also today's Sleep section).

Practical framing: favor interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and treat single-supplement "longevity" claims with skepticism.

sections.body:
A brand-new 2026 meta-analysis strengthens the case for HIIT as a **cardio** tool for women — while being honest about what it *doesn't* do on its own.

- **Big cardio win in mid-life and older women.** A 2026 systematic review & meta-analysis in *Frontiers in Physiology* (**19 RCTs**, searched through Nov 2025) found HIIT **significantly improved VO2max** vs. controls (SMD 1.20; high certainty of evidence), consistently across age groups, body-mass status, and program lengths.
- **But not a strength shortcut.** In the same analysis, HIIT did **not** significantly improve **muscle strength** (SMD −0.17) and only borderline improved walking ability (very low certainty) — so pair it with **resistance training** if strength and mobility are goals.
- **Recomposition over the scale.** A 2025 *Scientific Reports* meta-analysis in recreationally active women found HIIT produces small-but-real gains in VO2max and a **drop in body-fat %**, with **little change in total body mass** — expect recomposition, not big scale movement.
- **Reproductive-age nuance.** A meta-analysis of RCTs in women aged 18–35 found **MICT** (steady moderate cardio) slightly *outperformed* HIIT for pure cardiorespiratory fitness, with similar body-composition results — so a **blend** of HIIT and steady cardio is reasonable if you're younger.

Bottom line: intensity buys time-efficient cardio and fat-% improvements; **add strength work**, progress gradually, and keep recovery adequate.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). A fresh 2026 trial highlights just how powerful a structured, supervised program can be — even for women already scheduled for surgery.

- **Intensive pre-surgery PFMT delayed the OR.** An RCT in the *International Urogynecology Journal* (published **Mar 7, 2026**; 90 women awaiting mid-urethral sling surgery) compared a **6-week intensive preoperative PFMT** program to education alone. The PFMT group had significant gains in **muscle strength** (Modified Oxford, d=0.85) and **symptom severity** (Incontinence Severity Index, d=0.90) — and **43% postponed their planned surgery** afterward. Structured PFMT is a low-risk, low-cost step worth trying *before* an operation.
- **Supervised and consistent beats casual.** Long-standing evidence shows up to **~70% symptom improvement** with correctly performed PFMT, and that **supervised** programs (physiotherapist or continence nurse) of **at least 3 months** outperform unsupervised/leaflet-based care. A typical target: **≥8 contractions, 3×/day**.
- **Postmenopausal add-on.** A 2026 *Canadian Journal of Urology* RCT is examining **vaginal androgen + PFMT** vs. PFMT alone for postmenopausal SUI — part of growing interest in pairing local tissue support with training.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps.** Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback before ramping volume.

sections.topic: Targeted & Emerging Options — HER2+ / TP53 (p53) Breast Cancer
sections.body:
The most notable 2026 development for **p53 (TP53)-mutated** breast cancer isn't a supplement — it's a **first-in-class drug that reactivates broken p53**. "Alternative" here is best read as *emerging and integrative options discussed with your oncology team*, not replacements for standard care.

- **Rezatapopt — a p53 reactivator.** **Rezatapopt (PC14586)** is an investigational, oral, first-in-class small molecule that selectively binds the **TP53 Y220C** mutant protein and restores near-wild-type p53 function. In the phase 1 **PYNNACLE** study (published in the *NEJM*, reported March 2026; 77 heavily pretreated patients), the objective response rate was **20% overall** and **30%** among KRAS–wild-type patients dosed ≥1,150 mg/day, with responses **including breast cancer**. The most common side effects were nausea/vomiting; **2,000 mg once daily** was chosen for phase 2.
- **Phase 2 is enrolling a breast cohort.** **PYNNACLE (NCT04585750)** is now enrolling phase 2 cohorts — including a **breast cancer cohort (with HER2-positive disease)** — for TP53 Y220C-mutant, KRAS-wild-type tumors at 2,000 mg once daily with food. Eligibility hinges on tumor **next-generation sequencing**, so ask about genomic testing.
- **Why genetics matter here.** TP53 mutations occur in roughly **half of breast cancers** and drive more aggressive disease; germline TP53 changes are linked to early-onset HER2+ cancer. That makes **genomic testing** central to matching patients with trials like this one.

Important framing: this is **early (phase 1/2)** evidence in a **selected mutation** (Y220C). Treat it as a *targeted-therapy trial option* to raise with an oncologist — not a substitute for HER2-directed therapy, and separate from unproven "natural cure" claims.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or fragmented sleep, 2026 guidance keeps **behavioral therapy ahead of pills** — and is refreshingly clear about supplements.

- **CBT-I first, and often *enough*.** The **AASM's 2026** systematic review and guideline on *combination* therapy found that CBT-I **plus** medication beats **medication alone**, but combination is **not** better than **CBT-I alone** — because CBT-I delivers durable gains without drug risks. Core CBT-I tools: **sleep restriction, stimulus control, relaxation, and cognitive restructuring**.
- **If medication is needed, class matters.** **Dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs)** — **lemborexant, daridorexant, suvorexant** — help both **sleep onset and maintenance** and are generally better tolerated than older hypnotics. The phase-3 **SUNRISE 2** trial showed lemborexant sustained improvements over 6 months with mostly mild side effects. Guidelines support orexin antagonists for up to ~3 months.
- **Avoid the old standbys long-term.** Benzodiazepines and **Z-drugs** carry short- and long-term risks and are best avoided or kept **short-term** where possible.
- **Supplements, honestly.** Major guidelines **do not recommend standard melatonin** for chronic insomnia due to inconsistent efficacy — its clearest role is **circadian** problems (jet lag, shift work), and prolonged-release melatonin may be considered in adults **≥55**. Evidence for other OTC sleep aids is generally weak.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If fragmented sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
